new.title: Climb the Belfort for the dragon's view
new.desc: Ghent's 14th-century belfry was the city's strongbox and watchtower, and a gilded dragon still guards the top. From the gallery high above the Cloth Hall you look straight down on the three towers and the rooftops of the Kuip.
new.tip: There is a lift for most of the way, but take the stairs at least once to see the bells and the old drum of the carillon on your way up.

new.title: Wander the hilltop graves of Campo Santo
new.desc: Ghent's own Père Lachaise sits on a little hill in Sint-Amandsberg: a monumental cemetery full of sculpted tombs where many of the city's painters, writers and notables lie under old trees.
new.tip: Combine it with the Groot Begijnhof of Sint-Amandsberg a short walk away; the tram from the centre stops nearby.

new.title: Find the Rabot, the gate with its feet in the water
new.desc: This 15th-century fortified lock, with its two stubby round towers, once controlled the water flowing into the city. The canal it guarded no longer leads anywhere, which makes the little castle look charmingly out of place.
new.tip: Walk on to the Groot Begijnhof Sint-Elisabeth just beyond it for a quiet loop few visitors make.

new.title: Slip into the Begijnhof Ter Hoye
new.desc: Behind a gate on Lange Violettestraat lies a whole hidden village of whitewashed beguine houses, small streets and a church, part of the Flemish beguinages on the UNESCO list. The city noise simply stops.
new.tip: Keep your voice down: people live here. Go early in the morning for the stillest light on the courtyards.
new.q: Begijnhof Ter Hoye Lange Violettestraat Gent

new.title: Step into everyday life of old Flanders at Huis van Alijn
new.desc: Set in a medieval almshouse on the Kraanlei, this museum collects the ordinary stuff of Flemish life: toys, home photos, rituals and customs. It also has a traditional puppet theatre.
new.tip: Check the programme for a show by the house puppets; afterwards walk the courtyard and the Kraanlei facades.

new.title: Confront the history of madness at Museum Dr. Guislain
new.desc: Housed in Belgium's first purpose-built psychiatric hospital, still partly in use, this museum tells the story of how people with mental illness were treated, alongside striking outsider art exhibitions.
new.tip: It is a short tram ride north of the centre, so few tourists make it here. Allow time for the temporary exhibition, often the highlight.

new.title: Do art in stereo at S.M.A.K. and MSK
new.desc: In Citadelpark two museums face each other: MSK with Flemish masters from Bosch to Ensor, and S.M.A.K. with daring contemporary art. Ghent's arts quarter in one crossing of the street.
new.tip: Pick one for the morning, picnic in the park, then do the other. MSK also shows restored panels of the Ghent Altarpiece.

new.title: Escape the shopping street at Hotel d'Hane-Steenhuyse
new.desc: Behind a facade on the busy Veldstraat hides an 18th-century aristocratic town palace with painted salons, period furniture and a walled garden that feels miles away from the shops.
new.tip: It only opens on a few days each week; the Sunday morning guided tour also takes you into the nearby Arnold Vander Haeghen house and Maeterlinck's study.

new.title: Claim the bench in the Appelbrugparkje
new.desc: A pocket-sized riverside park tucked away behind Jan Breydelstraat, with a view across the Leie to the Groot Vleeshuis and the old Fish Market. Locals call it the most romantic corner of the city.
new.tip: Cross the new little fibreglass Appelbrugje footbridge and look back; Design Museum Gent is right opposite.

new.title: Look up at Van de Velde's Book Tower
new.desc: Henry van de Velde's 64-metre Boekentoren, the university library, is Ghent's fourth tower and a modernist icon. Its long renovation has brought it back to its clean concrete lines.
new.tip: From the Blandijnberg next to it you see the tower rise above the student quarter; check the university site for occasional tours to the Belvedere at the top.

new.title: Hear the looms at the Industriemuseum
new.desc: Ghent was the 'Manchester of the continent', and this museum in a former cotton mill (the old MIAT) shows how: working spinning machines, looms and print presses, plus the stories of the workers.
new.tip: Pick up the free walking map of the Old Docks here, since the self-guided harbour walk starts at the museum.

new.title: Eat Gentse stoverij on your fries at Frituur Tartaar
new.desc: Ghent's version of the Flemish beef and beer stew gets a slice of bread spread with Tierenteyn mustard, which makes it sharper and thicker. At Frituur Tartaar it comes poured over fries, with homemade tartar sauce on the side.
new.tip: The frituur is a few steps from the cathedral; ask for a local Ghent beer with it and eat on the spot.

new.title: Sip jenever at 't Dreupelkot
new.desc: A tiny bar by the water on the Groentenmarkt that pours around 200 jenevers, the Flemish gin, some of them flavoured in house. A 'dreupel' is a little drop, and that is how it is served.
new.tip: Let the bartender pick a fruit jenever for you, then try a classic old one to taste the difference.

new.title: Squeeze into the Galgenhuisje
new.desc: One of the smallest pubs in the city, wedged against the Groot Vleeshuis on the Groentenmarkt where the gallows once stood. Inside there is room for a handful of drinkers and a good choice of beers.
new.tip: If it's full upstairs, ask about the cellar; otherwise grab one of the few outside seats.

new.title: Fill a bag of old-fashioned sweets at Confiserie Temmerman
new.desc: A family sweet shop on the Kraanlei with jars of Ghent specialities like mokken, knopkes, cuberdons and the old 'poepkes'. The baroque facade shows the works of mercy in six relief panels.
new.tip: Ask what is typically Gents behind the counter; count the reliefs on the facade before you go in.

new.title: Drink at Dok Brewing Co. in a former transformer hall
new.desc: In the renewed Dok Noord area, a microbrewery and food hall fill a huge industrial hall, with outdoor seating along the old docks. A good taste of how Ghent's harbour is turning into a neighbourhood.
new.tip: Walk or cycle there along the Old Docks; on a sunny day the terrace by the water is the place to be.
new.q: Dok Brewing Company Dok Noord Gent

new.title: Eat a mastel at the Patersholfeesten
new.desc: Mastellen are round sweet bread rolls, eaten pressed with brown sugar. In August the Patershol throws its own neighbourhood party, and the mastellen come out with it.
new.tip: Ask for one 'gestreken' (ironed) with brown sugar so it caramelises; outside the festival, look for them at Ghent bakeries.

new.title: Have a beer by the water at De Geus van Gent
new.desc: A student-quarter pub on the Kantienberg with a short, good beer list and seats along the river, far from the tourist terraces.
new.tip: It opens late in the afternoon and closes on Sundays; come at sunset when the quay catches the last light.
new.q: De Geus van Gent Kantienberg Gent

new.title: See the city from a canal boat
new.desc: Ghent was built on water, and a short boat trip from the Graslei and Korenlei glides past guild houses, the castle and the hidden backs of medieval houses you never see from the street.
new.tip: Sit on the outside edge of the boat for photos, and duck when the guide warns of the low bridges.

new.title: Paddle and stroll around the Old Docks
new.desc: The former harbour docks Houtdok, Handelsdok and Achterdok have become a new waterside district, with houseboats, harbour cranes, a park and a canoe rental right on the Houtdok.
new.tip: Follow the self-guided Old Docks walk that starts from the Industriemuseum, or rent a canoe and see the docks from the water.

new.title: Swim in the lake at the Blaarmeersen
new.desc: On the west side of the city, Ghent's big sports and recreation park has a lake with beaches, plus a climbing wall and watersports. It's where Gentenaars go on the first hot day of the year.
new.tip: On busy summer days you may need to book the beach in advance; cycle there along the water from the centre.

new.title: Hunt for curiosities at the Bij Sint-Jacobs flea market
new.desc: Every Friday, Saturday and Sunday morning, the square around the Romanesque Sint-Jacobskerk fills with stalls of old lamps, trinkets, records and odd bits of Ghent households.
new.tip: Go early for the best finds, then browse the vintage and antique shops in the surrounding streets.

new.title: Read with a view at De Krook
new.desc: The city library stacks its floors in a striking building on the Schelde, with a reading café, a study room and tech to try out. Below it, the Nelson Mandelapromenade is a green quay to sit by the water.
new.tip: Grab a newspaper, find a window seat on an upper floor, then rent a bike at the bike point under the building.

new.title: Sing along with the Buffalos at a KAA Gent match
new.desc: Ghent's first-division football club plays in a 20,000-seat stadium on the south side of town. The blue-and-white crowd, nicknamed the Buffalos, makes match day a proper local ritual.
new.tip: Cycle or take the train to Gent Sint-Pieters and walk; the bike parking at the stadium is part of the experience.

new.title: Admire the lace-like town hall of Oudenaarde
new.desc: Oudenaarde's flamboyant Gothic town hall and belfry on the Markt are on the UNESCO belfry list. Inside, the MOU museum shows the famous Oudenaarde tapestries the town once exported across Europe.
new.tip: Trains from Ghent take about half an hour; pair it with the Centrum Ronde van Vlaanderen on the same square.

new.title: Meet the older Manneken Pis in Geraardsbergen
new.desc: Geraardsbergen claims its little peeing boy in front of the town hall is the oldest Manneken Pis, about 160 years older than the one in Brussels. He even has his own small museum with his costumes.
new.tip: The museum is in the tourist office in the old Cloth Hall next door; afterwards climb the Muur to the chapel on the Oudenberg.

new.title: Descend into the Romanesque crypt of Ronse
new.desc: Under the Sint-Hermesbasiliek in Ronse lies a forest of columns from the 11th century, built for the relics of Saint Hermes, patron of people with nervous and mental illness. Pilgrims came here for centuries seeking healing.
new.tip: Audio guides are available; look for the original Romanesque columns with cube capitals among the later ones. Ronse is reachable by train from Ghent via Oudenaarde.

new.title: Walk the UNESCO beguinage of Dendermonde
new.desc: Sixty-one small houses, most from the 1600s, stand around a green trapezium square in the Sint-Alexiusbegijnhof. It is one of the Flemish beguinages on the UNESCO list and has a small museum on beguine life.
new.tip: Combine it with the belfry and town hall on the Grote Markt, and finish with a local Vicaris beer.

new.title: See the Renaissance towers of Ooidonk on the Leie
new.desc: Near Deinze, in a loop of the Leie, Kasteel Ooidonk rises from its moat with bulb-topped towers. Rebuilt in Renaissance style in 1592, it is still lived in by a noble family.
new.tip: The castle itself only opens in spring and summer, but the park with its French garden can be visited all year. Cycle there along the Leie from Ghent.

new.title: Learn the begonia story at the Lochristi horticulture museum
new.desc: Lochristi grew rich on begonias and azaleas, and its Begoniafestival once drew crowds from far away. The LoS museum in the old presbytery of Zaffelare tells that story among greenhouses and old tools.
new.tip: The museum opens on the last full weekend of the month from March to October, but its garden is free to visit any day.

new.title: Taste an Aalsterse vlaai
new.desc: Aalst has its own vlaai, a dense, dark, spiced bread pudding baked by the town's bakeries. It is the local treat that has nothing to do with the Limburg fruit tarts of the same name.
new.tip: Buy a slice from one of the bakeries in the centre or at the Saturday market, and eat it on the Grote Markt by the old Schepenhuis.

new.title: Visit the Filliers jenever distillery by the Leie
new.desc: Since 1880 the Filliers family has distilled grain jenever in Bachte-Maria-Leerne near Deinze, one of the last big names of the Flemish gin tradition.
new.tip: Visits and tastings are for groups or by booking, so plan ahead; combine with a ride along the Leie to Ooidonk castle.

new.title: Have a drink at the old lock of Astene
new.desc: Het Oud Sashuis is a cosy café beside the iron sluice of Astene, built in 1876 to tame Leie floods. In summer the terrace looks right out over the river.
new.tip: It makes a perfect stop on a bike ride from Ghent along the Leie via Sint-Martens-Latem to Deinze.

new.title: Eat paardenworst in Lokeren
new.desc: Lokeren is known for its horse meat sausage, the local speciality that turns up at butchers and in cafés across town.
new.tip: Ask for it at a butcher near the Markt and eat it with bread and mustard. If you come in early August, the Lokerse Feesten music festival fills the town.

new.title: Drink an Adriaen Brouwer from Brouwerij Roman in Mater
new.desc: Founded in 1545 in an inn on an old trade route, Roman in Mater near Oudenaarde is one of the oldest family breweries in Belgium, now run by the 14th generation. Its brown Adriaen Brouwer is the classic Oudenaards bruin.
new.tip: Ask for it in the cafés of Oudenaarde and compare it with a Liefmans; Mater is a pleasant cycle into the Flemish Ardennes.

new.title: Catch a krakeling on the Oudenberg in Geraardsbergen
new.desc: At the end of February a historic procession climbs the Oudenberg and thousands of krakelingen (ring-shaped rolls) are thrown down from the top; one hides a note worth a golden krakeling. In the evening a straw barrel is burned to chase away winter.
new.tip: Stand on the slope below the chapel and bring something to hold your catch. The live-fish drinking ritual has been dropped since 2026.

new.title: Hike the Kluisbos on the Kluisberg
new.desc: A hilly beech forest straddling the language border in the Flemish Ardennes, full of springs, wild hyacinths in spring and two big ironsand stones locals call Peetje en Meetje, said to be an old offering table.
new.tip: Several long-distance trails cross the forest; come in late April for the bluebells, and wear real shoes on the steep, muddy slopes.

new.title: Cycle the creeks of the Meetjesland around the Boerekreek
new.desc: In the north of the Meetjesland, medieval storm floods left a web of creeks with sharp bends and deep pools. The Boerekreek in Sint-Jan-in-Eremo is the largest, a winding water edged with reeds and polders.
new.tip: Bring or rent a bike in Eeklo and follow the cycle network north through the polders toward Sint-Laureins and Boekhoute.

new.title: Walk the dike around the Molsbroek in Lokeren
new.desc: A marshland reserve on the edge of Lokeren where water birds gather among reed beds, alder woods and wet meadows, part of the Scheldt valley national park.
new.tip: A paved 4.5 km dike loops around the whole reserve; start at the visitor centre on Molsbergenstraat and bring binoculars.

new.title: Take a dip in the Vosselare Put
new.desc: A former bend of the Leie near Deinze where swimming in natural water is allowed in summer, a rare thing in Flanders.
new.tip: Open only in the swimming season; cycle from Ghent along the Leie and stop at the Astene lock on the way.
